text: The capstone's content is done. This closing lesson of Chapter 5 is about the step that turns a finished draft into a genuinely stronger piece of work: having someone else read it critically, and actually revising based on what they find.

This lesson covers why peer review is a core part of real research practice, a structured self-review pass you can run before anyone else sees your work, what to actually ask a reviewer for so their feedback is useful, and how to triage feedback once you receive it.

Every paper you learned to read critically back in Chapter 1 went through some form of review before publication. Re-read your own report the same way: does the summary's claim match what the results section's numbers actually support? Is every hypothesis claim addressed explicitly in the conclusions, including any that weren't fully supported? Does the limitations section name every confound and scope boundary you know about, not just the convenient ones?

Vague requests like 'can you look this over' produce vague feedback. Ask specifically: does my methods section give you enough detail to attempt a replication, testing specificity on your own writing; does my conclusion claim anything my results don't actually support, testing scoping discipline; and is there anywhere you got confused or had to re-read a sentence, catching clarity problems you can't easily see in your own familiar writing.

Sort incoming comments into three categories. Must-fix: a factual error, an unsupported claim, a genuinely unclear methods step — fix these before considering the report final. Worth considering: a suggestion that would improve clarity but isn't strictly required. Noted but not changing: a stylistic preference you disagree with, or something outside your project's scope — it's fine to note you considered it and chose not to act, rather than silently ignoring it or treating every comment as mandatory.

Chapter 6 closes this entire fourteen-course path with an honest look at where the real jobs are — starting next lesson with what the quantum computing job market actually looks like today, not the version implied by popular coverage of the field.
